Participants felt older after taking a memory test ( M = 54.79 years, SD = 16.79) than at baseline ( M = 50.04 years, SD = 13.80), t (27) = 2.71, SE = 1.75; d = 0.76, 95% CI = [0.33, 1.18]. ... notes: Identity independently verified in supplied canonical text: Aging 5 Years in 5 Minutes: The Effect of Taking a Memory Test on Older Adults’ Subjective Age; Matthew L Hughes, Lisa Geraci, Ross L De Forrest; DOI 10.1177/0956797613494853; Psychol Sci 24(12):2481–2488 (2013). Primary author manuscript hosted in PMC; full-text parse includes all four studies, methods/results, discussion, footnotes and references, not merely an abstract or secondary summary. No PDF supplied; no PDF rendering possible. Only pval_value_o assigned; all other fields are placeholders. Multiple Study 3 d-bearing comparisons fit the study-only locator: baseline subjective versus chronological age (d=0.95), between-group chronological age (d=0.33, p=.24), and memory-condition subjective-age change (d=0.76). Note 1 supplies p<.05 for the first and third candidates through its article-wide significance convention, without exact p values. The blank description and p.5 locator do not distinguish these tests. No target selected by numeric matching or row order; no p calculated from statistics. Study 3 also reports a time main effect p=.08 and a significant test-type/time interaction with partial eta squared .10. These are distinct tests and cannot supply the p for an unspecified d-bearing comparison.
